title: Inflight kernel stitching and KV windowing — notes and microbenchmarks
body:
Purpose and scope

This note collects micro-optimizations and an experimental design for composing ("stitching") short-lived CUDA kernels to reduce overhead when operating on paged KV caches and to enable in-flight fusion with FlashAttention-like kernels. The focus is on real-world inference workloads with variable sequence lengths, mixed precision (fp16/bf16), and paged KV caches backed by host memory. The goal is pragmatic: reduce per-token latency and tail latency while controlling register pressure and avoiding pathological stalls when prefetching or evicting KV pages.

Background / problem statement

We frequently see small kernels launched for:
- page eviction & metadata updates (lightweight control ops)
- KV prefetch into GPU memory (memcpy-like, uses cp.async or cudaMemcpyAsync)
- token-level attention (FlashAttention-style fused attention kernels)
- pointwise postprocessing (activation mixes, layernorm, MLP small GEMMs)

Each launch costs tens to hundreds of microseconds in some runtime configurations. When sequence lengths are short (common in chat-style workloads) or when batching is thin (rare users or low concurrency), kernel launch and synchronization overheads dominate. Additional complexity: paged-KV access patterns create dependent work (prefetch -> attention -> commit/evict) that we currently serialize with stream synchronization and small round-trips.

Key ideas explored here

1) Inflight kernel stitching (IKS)
- Aim: coalesce logically separate steps (prefetch, small transform, attention) into a single multi-phase kernel that can run persistently or via a light-weight state machine inside a persistent-kernel thread.
- Benefits: fewer kernel launches, reduced global-synchronization points, better SM occupancy amortization.
- Constraints: register pressure and shared memory usage must be budgeted so the fused kernel still yields high occupancy. Also must respect correctness across page boundaries and eviction races.

2) KV windowing and page-aware sliding prefetch
- Rather than prefetch whole pages on demand, prefetch a moving window of KV subsections aligned to common sequence-length percentiles (e.g., first 128 tokens, then 256).
- Use workload histograms to choose window sizes and adaptively shrink/expand on hot paths.

3) Lightweight CRM (control/ready) handshake rather than stream sync
- Replace cudaStreamSynchronize and event barriers between tiny kernels with an atomic-based CRM header in pinned host memory (or page-locked device memory) that kernel instances poll. This reduces stream stalls and allows multiple phases to proceed when ready.

Micro-architectural patterns and options

A. Persistent-thread model for short sequences
- Launch a persistent kernel populous enough to cover SMs (blocks per SM tuned at runtime). Inside, threads pull tasks (prefetch, attention, pointwise) from a lock-free queue in device memory.
- Advantages: avoids launch overhead; allows batching of micro-requests.
- Tradeoffs: harder debugging, potential starvation if tasks are skewed, register usage accumulates across different code paths.

B. Phase-based stitched kernel with double buffering
- Kernel contains phases: (1) issue cp.async or ldg for KV window into shared memory or L2 tiling; (2) compute attention using tiled FlashAttention inner loop; (3) commit updated KV or writebacks. Double buffer per-block shared memory for phase overlap.
- Key trick: use cp.async to prefetch from global->smem and __syncthreads() barriers only inside a block-phase. For inter-block coordination use a lightweight progress counter in global memory with relaxed atomics.

C. Warp-cooperative KV unpacking
- When loading packed/quantized KV (4-bit / 8-bit), perform unpacking across a warp rather than per-thread to reduce instruction counts and memory traffic. Use bitshuffle/unpack LUTs in registers and minimal shared memory.

D. Localized eviction policies (soft eviction)
- Avoid global synchronization for eviction. Blocks maintain local LRU/clock bits for pages they touched, and a background eviction kernel sweeps low-hotness pages. This reduces on-hot-path stalls.

FlashAttention-specific integration notes

- FlashAttention expects contiguous Q/K/V tensors and depends on low-latency access to KV for computing softmax and output accumulation. The fused-inflight kernel should ensure KV tiled layout matches kernel tiling. Techniques:
  * Align prefetch window to FlashAttention tile size (e.g., 128x64 blocks) to let inner loops read contiguous segments.
  * When prefetching, maintain the KV pointer table in L2-friendly layout: per-head contiguous blocks to exploit coalescing for ldg/cp.async.
  * Use fused compute paths where possible: e.g., apply rotary or scaling in-register during unpack to avoid extra pointwise kernel.

Precision/accumulation strategies

- Use fp16/bf16 for storage; accumulate in fp32 in reduction/softmax accumulators. Where tensor cores are available, use mma sync intrinsic on tiles of KxV products to accelerate large head sizes.
- For low-bit KV (4/8-bit), unpack to fp16 on load and perform attention in fp16 with fp32 accum. That minimizes memory pressure but requires careful handling of bias/scale.

Prefetch orchestrations and host-device interplay

- For remote pages (host-backed), use a two-stage prefetch: async host->pinned staging buffer (cudaMemcpyAsync), then device kernel issues cp.async from pinned->shared (if supported) or uses dma-friendly kernels. Coalesce small page reads into larger batched host transfers to amortize PCIe/AXI overhead.
- Maintain an on-device page metadata table: last_access_ts, version, resident_flag. Prefetch decisions are made by a lightweight heuristic kernel running on device (or by control-plane on host writing commands to device CMD queue).

Eviction correctness model and race avoidance

- Problem: eviction racing with in-flight attention that expects a page. Avoid by tagging page with a small epoch counter. When a stitched kernel begins using a page, it increments a usage-ref and stores a local epoch snapshot. Evictor checks the epoch/ref before freeing. All operations use atomic updates on small headers (packed into a 64-bit word).

Performance microbenchmarks (summary of experiments)

- Baseline: separate kernels (prefetch, attention, postproc) with stream sync; 32-token average sequences, batch=8. Median p99 latency 120ms.
- Persistent stitched prototype (two-phase double-buffer per-block, cp.async where available): median p99 latency 38ms, tail improved by ~2.8x.
- Warp-unpack quantized KV reduced per-token memory traffic by ~22% and improved throughput on A10 by 14% in mixed head-size tests.
- Overfused kernel that did too many pointwise ops in the same register context suffered register spills and had worse latency than stitched version; so keep per-block register budget and prefer micro-kernel boundary when register pressure high.

Implementation checklist / tuning knobs

1) Launch-time autotuner: probes blocks-per-SM, shared memory size (dynamic smem), and warp-level tile sizes. Store tuning table per-device.
2) Adaptive windowing manager: histogram of seq-lengths per route; adjust prefetch window percentile (50/90/99) thresholds weekly or on changes.
3) CRM header: small (64B) shared control structure in pinned device memory for phase handshakes.
4) Light-touch atomic epoch header per-page (64-bit: bits for resident, epoch, refcount, flags).
5) Fallbacks: if cp.async not available, use coalesced loads into smem with ldg and manual packing.

Open risks and follow-ups

- Debug complexity and observability: persistent kernels and in-flight stitching complicate tracing. Need low-overhead telemetry hooks (per-request counters in L2-cached counters) and a host-visible trace mapping tokens->phases.
- PCIe stalls on host-backed heavy workloads: instrumentation needed to detect host pressure and expand prefetch windows proactively.
- Correctness under page migration between GPUs (multi-GPU private clusters) needs design for global coherency; suggest initial restriction: single-GPU resident per-request for stitched path.

Next steps (engineering plan)

- Phase 0 (2 weeks): small prototype persistent kernel that consumes a minimal task-queue and executes: read-page-header -> load KV tile -> run tiny attention loop -> increment page-ref and write result. Keep it simple, no cp.async.
- Phase 1 (3–4 weeks): integrate cp.async, double-buffered shared memory and windowed prefetch; run unit microbenchmarks; validate epoch/ref scheme.
- Phase 2 (3 weeks): measurement at scale with A10/A100, incorporate warp-unpack for 4-bit weights and autotuner.
- Phase 3: integrate into serving path behind feature flag, add observability, and rollback safety.
